claim: Helicases utilize nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) hydrolysis to translocate along single-stranded nucleic acids (NA) and unwind the duplex.
source: Helicases utilize nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) hydrolysis to translocate along single-stranded nucleic acids (NA) and unwind the duplex.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about helicase function.

claim: In the cell, helicases function in the context of other NA-associated proteins such as single-stranded DNA binding proteins.
source: In the cell, helicases function in the context of other NA-associated proteins such as single-stranded DNA binding proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cellular context of helicase function.

claim: Encounters with other NA-associated proteins regulate helicase function.
source: Such encounters regulate helicase function, although the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact, though mechanisms are unknown.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of how encounters with other proteins regulate helicase function remain largely unknown.
source: Such encounters regulate helicase function, although the underlying mechanisms remain largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Ferroplasma acidarmanus xeroderma pigmentosum group D (XPD) helicase serves as a model for understanding the molecular mechanisms of superfamily 2B helicases.
source: Ferroplasma acidarmanus xeroderma pigmentosum group D (XPD) helicase serves as a model for understanding the molecular mechanisms of superfamily 2B helicases, and its activity is enhanced by the cognate single-stranded DNA binding protein replication protein A 2 (RPA2).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about the model system used.

claim: XPD activity is enhanced by the cognate single-stranded DNA binding protein replication protein A 2 (RPA2).
source: Ferroplasma acidarmanus xeroderma pigmentosum group D (XPD) helicase serves as a model for understanding the molecular mechanisms of superfamily 2B helicases, and its activity is enhanced by the cognate single-stranded DNA binding protein replication protein A 2 (RPA2).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact and is also supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Optical trap measurements reveal that XPD interconverts between two states with different processivities.
source: Here, optical trap measurements of the unwinding activity of a single XPD helicase in the presence of RPA2 reveal a mechanism in which XPD interconverts between two states with different processivities and transient RPA2 interactions stabilize the more processive state, activating a latent 'processivity switch' in XPD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Transient RPA2 interactions stabilize the more processive state of XPD.
source: Here, optical trap measurements of the unwinding activity of a single XPD helicase in the presence of RPA2 reveal a mechanism in which XPD interconverts between two states with different processivities and transient RPA2 interactions stabilize the more processive state, activating a latent 'processivity switch' in XPD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: RPA2 interactions activate a latent 'processivity switch' in XPD.
source: Here, optical trap measurements of the unwinding activity of a single XPD helicase in the presence of RPA2 reveal a mechanism in which XPD interconverts between two states with different processivities and transient RPA2 interactions stabilize the more processive state, activating a latent 'processivity switch' in XPD.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A point mutation at a regulatory DNA binding site on XPD activates the processivity switch.
source: A point mutation at a regulatory DNA binding site on XPD similarly activates this switch.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A large class of helicases unwind by translocating directionally along a single NA strand.
source: A large class of helicases unwind by translocating directionally along a single NA strand and can utilize this translocation activity to displace NA-bound proteins (Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2002; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2003; Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Helicases can utilize translocation activity to displace NA-bound proteins.
source: A large class of helicases unwind by translocating directionally along a single NA strand and can utilize this translocation activity to displace NA-bound proteins (Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2002; Delagoutte and von Hippel, 2003; Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Helicases are involved in many essential genome maintenance processes, including replication, recombination, and repair.
source: In the cell, helicases are involved in many essential genome maintenance processes, including replication, recombination, and repair (McGlynn, 2013; Daley et al., 2013; Kuper and Kisker, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The same helicase is known to carry out several disparate functions.
source: In a number of instances, the same helicase is known to carry out several of these disparate functions (Lohman et al., 2008; Wu and Spies, 2013; Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Helicase activity must be tightly regulated to prevent indiscriminate unwinding of duplex DNA in the cell, which could lead to genome instability.
source: Thus, helicase activity must be tightly regulated not only to prevent indiscriminate unwinding of duplex DNA in the cell, which could lead to genome instability, but also to define the context-dependent role of the helicase.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the consequences of unregulated helicase activity.

claim: Helicase activity must be regulated to define the context-dependent role of the helicase.
source: Thus, helicase activity must be tightly regulated not only to prevent indiscriminate unwinding of duplex DNA in the cell, which could lead to genome instability, but also to define the context-dependent role of the helicase.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the multiple functions of helicases.

claim: Growing evidence points to interactions with protein partners as one regulatory mechanism for helicases.
source: How this regulation occurs is often unclear, but growing evidence points to interactions with protein partners as one regulatory mechanism (Lohman et al., 2008; Wu and Spies, 2013; Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: XPD protein is a 5′ to 3′ DNA helicase.
source: Xeroderma pigmentosum group D (XPD) protein is a 5′ to 3′ DNA helicase that serves as a model for understanding members of the structural superfamily 2B of helicases, a group that includes yeast Rad3 and human FANCJ, RTEL, and CHLR1 (Fairman-Williams et al., 2010; Byrd, 2012; White and Dillingham, 2012; Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Structural superfamily 2B of helicases includes yeast Rad3 and human FANCJ, RTEL, and CHLR1.
source: Xeroderma pigmentosum group D (XPD) protein is a 5′ to 3′ DNA helicase that serves as a model for understanding members of the structural superfamily 2B of helicases, a group that includes yeast Rad3 and human FANCJ, RTEL, and CHLR1 (Fairman-Williams et al., 2010; Byrd, 2012; White and Dillingham, 2012; Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human XPD is part of transcription factor IIH.
source: Human XPD is part of transcription factor IIH and plays a vital role in nucleotide excision repair (Egly and Coin, 2011; Fuss and Tainer, 2011; Kuper et al., 2014; Houten et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human XPD plays a vital role in nucleotide excision repair.
source: Human XPD is part of transcription factor IIH and plays a vital role in nucleotide excision repair (Egly and Coin, 2011; Fuss and Tainer, 2011; Kuper et al., 2014; Houten et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: XPD has been shown to participate in chromosome segregation.
source: It has also been shown to participate in chromosome segregation (Ito et al., 2010) and in the cell's defense against retroviral infection (Yoder et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: XPD participates in the cell's defense against retroviral infection.
source: It has also been shown to participate in chromosome segregation (Ito et al., 2010) and in the cell's defense against retroviral infection (Yoder et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: XPD consists of a conserved motor core comprising helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2) that couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to translocation on ssDNA.
source: Structurally, XPD consists of a conserved motor core (Figure 1a)—helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2)—that couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to translocation on ssDNA, an FeS cluster-containing domain, and a unique ARCH domain that encircles the translocating strand (Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Wolski et al., 2008; Kuper et al., 2012; Spies, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: XPD contains an FeS cluster-containing domain.
source: Structurally, XPD consists of a conserved motor core (Figure 1a)—helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2)—that couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to translocation on ssDNA, an FeS cluster-containing domain, and a unique ARCH domain that encircles the translocating strand (Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Wolski et al., 2008; Kuper et al., 2012; Spies, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: XPD has a unique ARCH domain that encircles the translocating strand.
source: Structurally, XPD consists of a conserved motor core (Figure 1a)—helicase domains 1 and 2 (HD1 and HD2)—that couples ATP binding and hydrolysis to translocation on ssDNA, an FeS cluster-containing domain, and a unique ARCH domain that encircles the translocating strand (Fan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Wolski et al., 2008; Kuper et al., 2012; Spies, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: FacXPD unwinding is enhanced greatly by FacRPA2.
source: Prior work (Pugh et al., 2008) has shown that FacXPD unwinding is enhanced greatly by one type of cognate ssDNA binding protein in F. acidarmanus, RPA2, more so than a second cognate protein, RPA1, or by heterologous proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FacRPA2 enhances FacXPD unwinding more than RPA1 or heterologous proteins.
source: Prior work (Pugh et al., 2008) has shown that FacXPD unwinding is enhanced greatly by one type of cognate ssDNA binding protein in F. acidarmanus, RPA2, more so than a second cognate protein, RPA1, or by heterologous proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FacRPA2 has a simple, single-domain architecture with one OB-fold that occludes ~4 nt of ssDNA.
source: FacRPA2 has a simple, single-domain architecture with one OB-fold that occludes ~4 nt of ssDNA (Figure 1b; Pugh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: Single-molecule experiments demonstrated that XPD can occupy the same DNA strand as RPA2 and bypass RPA2-bound ssDNA.
source: Single-molecule experiments demonstrated that XPD can occupy the same DNA strand as RPA2 and bypass RPA2-bound ssDNA (Honda et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No direct, specific interactions between RPA2 and XPD in solution have been observed.
source: Crucially, no direct, specific interactions between RPA2 and XPD in solution have been observed (Pugh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: XPD processivity increases with RPA2 concentration.
source: XPD processivity increases with RPA2 concentration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the figure caption for Figure 1d and supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: XPD unwound in repeated 'bursts', comprising cycles of forward unwinding motion followed by backward rezipping.
source: As previously reported, XPD unwound in repeated 'bursts', comprising cycles of forward unwinding motion followed by backward rezipping (Qi et al., 2013), repeating a number of times (5 ± 1) until the protein dissociated (e.g., t = 95 s for 0 nM RPA2 or t = 160 s for 2 nM RPA2 in Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: XPD bursts repeat a number of times (5 ± 1) until the protein dissociated.
source: As previously reported, XPD unwound in repeated 'bursts', comprising cycles of forward unwinding motion followed by backward rezipping (Qi et al., 2013), repeating a number of times (5 ± 1) until the protein dissociated (e.g., t = 95 s for 0 nM RPA2 or t = 160 s for 2 nM RPA2 in Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Unwinding never resumed once a dissociation event occurred, indicating that the single molecule of XPD was flushed away in the flow chamber.
source: Unwinding never resumed once a dissociation event occurred, indicating that the single molecule of XPD was flushed away in the flow chamber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that unwinding never resumed after dissociation.

claim: In the absence of RPA2, the processivity of XPD was low, on average 15–20 out of 89 bp.
source: In the absence of RPA2, we observe that the processivity—the maximum hairpin position reached by XPD during any one burst—was low, on average 15–20 out of 89 bp, consistent with our prior work (Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data in the manuscript and citation to prior work.

claim: With increasing [RPA2], XPD unwound farther into the hairpin, occasionally unwinding the entire 89 bp hairpin stem.
source: With increasing [RPA2], XPD unwound farther into the hairpin, occasionally unwinding the entire 89 bp hairpin stem (e.g., t = 20 s for 5 nM RPA2 or t = 30 s, 70 s for 50 nM RPA2 in Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Processivity varied greatly from burst to burst.
source: Each burst represents an attempt by one XPD molecule to unwind the hairpin, and we found that processivity varied greatly from burst to burst.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: XPD can backstep or backslide via temporary disengagement from the unwinding DNA strand.
source: As shown in the representative trace in Figure 2a, several molecular events comprised backward motion: XPD backstepping or backsliding via temporary disengagement from the unwinding DNA strand (Figure 2b, diagrams 1a and 1b), or translocation on the other hairpin strand away from the fork junction (2 and 3), all leading to DNA rezipping under its regression force.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: XPD can translocate on the other hairpin strand away from the fork junction, leading to DNA rezipping.
source: As shown in the representative trace in Figure 2a, several molecular events comprised backward motion: XPD backstepping or backsliding via temporary disengagement from the unwinding DNA strand (Figure 2b, diagrams 1a and 1b), or translocation on the other hairpin strand away from the fork junction (2 and 3), all leading to DNA rezipping under its regression force.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: XPD can completely unwind the hairpin stem and translocate past the dT tetraloop cap onto the opposing strand, allowing the stem to rezip gradually in the protein's wake.
source: An example of the latter occurred when XPD completely unwound the hairpin stem and translocated past the dT tetraloop cap onto the opposing strand, allowing the stem to rezip gradually in the protein's wake (Figure 2b, diagram 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a and 2b.

claim: Gradual rezipping of the duplex mid-hairpin is attributed to XPD disengaging from its DNA strand to switch to the opposing strand.
source: In a contrasting example, we observed gradual rezipping of the duplex mid-hairpin, which we attributed to XPD disengaging from its DNA strand to switch to the opposing strand (Figure 2b, diagram 3), a behavior reported for other helicases (Dessinges et al., 2004; Comstock et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to similar behavior in other helicases.

claim: Gradual rezipping was typically followed by a stall at ~10 bp, consistent with the protein stalling at the abasic site on the 3′ strand at the base of the hairpin.
source: This interpretation is corroborated by the observation that gradual rezipping was typically followed by a stall at ~10 bp (Figure 2a, t = 58 s) the size of XPD's footprint, consistent with the protein stalling at the abasic site on the 3′ strand at the base of the hairpin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the known footprint of XPD.

claim: Subsequent unwinding bursts were presumably due to XPD strand-switching back to the original strand.
source: Subsequent unwinding bursts were presumably due to XPD strand-switching back to the original strand.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Rapid rezipping events due to backsliding usually occurred to the base of the hairpin, consistent with the protein remaining on the hairpin 5′ strand.
source: In contrast, rapid rezipping events due to backsliding usually occurred to the base of the hairpin (Figure 2a, t = 44 s), consistent with the protein remaining on the hairpin 5′ strand.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: The mean processivity increases with RPA2 concentration from 19 bp at 0 nM RPA2 to 35 bp at 50 nM RPA2.
source: When unwinding in the presence of RPA2, the average burst processivity increases with [RPA2] from 19 bp at 0 nM RPA2 to 35 bp at 50 nM RPA2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: As [RPA2] increases, an increasing fraction of bursts fall into a higher processivity tail of the distribution, which includes many cases of complete unwinding of the 89 bp hairpin.
source: As [RPA2] increases, an increasing fraction of bursts fall into a higher processivity tail of the distribution, which includes many cases of complete unwinding of the 89 bp hairpin.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The distribution of burst processivity for all [RPA2] shows a large population of bursts with average processivity of 15–20 bp, followed by a long tail with processivity extending from 25 to 89 bp.
source: The distribution of burst processivity for all [RPA2] (Figure 2d) shows a large population of bursts with average processivity of 15–20 bp, followed by a long tail with processivity extending from 25 to 89 bp.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: RPA2 is capable of transiently destabilizing hairpin DNA under force of 12 pN.
source: As shown in Figure 3a, RPA2 is capable of transiently destabilizing hairpin DNA under force of 12 pN.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: In experiments with RPA2 but without XPD, short melting events are observed, corresponding to the hairpin opening by ~5–6 bp, comparable to the footprint of RPA2.
source: In experiments with RPA2 but without XPD, short melting events are observed, corresponding to the hairpin opening by ~5–6 bp, comparable to the footprint of RPA2 (Pugh et al., 2008), and reannealing shortly thereafter (~20 ms).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3a and citation to prior work.

claim: RPA2-mediated melting events become more frequent as the concentration of RPA2 is increased.
source: These melting events become more frequent as the concentration of RPA2 is increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), in support of melting being RPA2-mediated.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An effective second-order rate constant of (1.2 ± 0.3)×10^8 M^−1 s^−1 is estimated for RPA2 binding.
source: Analyzing the times between melting events, we estimate an effective second-order rate constant of (1.2 ± 0.3)×108 M−1 s−1 for binding.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the data.

claim: RPA2-mediated melting events are observable as XPD unwinds in the presence of RPA2.
source: RPA2-mediated melting events are also observable as XPD unwinds in the presence of RPA2 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: RPA2 is capable of binding at the same fork junction as XPD and melting DNA ahead of the helicase.
source: This finding indicates that RPA2 is capable of binding at the same fork junction as XPD and melting DNA ahead of the helicase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of RPA2 melting events during XPD unwinding.

claim: After a melting event, the hairpin is most likely to reanneal all the way back to the same position as before the event, indicating that XPD has not moved from its initial position.
source: After a melting event, we find that the hairpin is most likely to reanneal all the way back to the same position as before the event, indicating that XPD has not moved from its initial position.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: There is no significant forward movement of XPD as a result of RPA2 duplex melting.
source: Importantly, this result shows that there is no significant forward movement of XPD as a result of RPA2 duplex melting, and that XPD does not exploit RPA2's melting activity to enhance its own unwinding.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: XPD does not exploit RPA2's melting activity to enhance its own unwinding.
source: Importantly, this result shows that there is no significant forward movement of XPD as a result of RPA2 duplex melting, and that XPD does not exploit RPA2's melting activity to enhance its own unwinding.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: As force is decreased, RPA2-mediated melting occurs less frequently, with almost no melting detected at 9 pN and below.
source: As force is decreased, RPA2-mediated melting occurs less frequently, with almost no melting detected at 9 pN and below (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: XPD activity was enhanced by RPA2 at 9 pN, with a significantly higher fraction of bursts with processivities in the long tail extending from 25 to 89 bp.
source: However, XPD activity was enhanced by RPA2 at 9 pN (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with a significantly higher fraction of bursts with processivities in the long tail extending from 25 to 89 bp.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At forces of 7–8 pN and a concentration of 250 nM gp32 melts the hairpin transiently by ~5–10 bp, comparable to RPA2 at 12 pN.
source: We determined that at forces of 7–8 pN and a concentration of 250 nM gp32 melts the hairpin transiently by ~5–10 bp, comparable to RPA2 at 12 pN (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a.

claim: gp32 has a minimal impact on XPD processivity under conditions where it melts the hairpin to a similar extent as RPA2.
source: However, gp32 has a minimal impact on XPD processivity under these conditions. We observed no bursts in the >25 bp, high-processivity tail of the distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b), in marked contrast to the corresponding conditions with RPA2 (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4b.

claim: Enhancement of XPD processivity by RPA2 is mediated by a mechanism other than duplex melting.
source: Taken together, these data strongly indicate that enhancement of XPD processivity by RPA2 is mediated by a mechanism other than duplex melting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that melting does not correlate with processivity enhancement.

claim: The fraction of bursts categorized as high processivity increases clearly with RPA2 concentration, saturating to ~50% at RPA2 concentrations >10 nM.
source: The fraction of bursts categorized as high processivity increases clearly with RPA2 concentration (Figure 4a) saturating to ~50% at RPA2 concentrations >10 nM (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: Long stalls (sometimes exceeding tens of seconds in duration) around 10–15 bp are evident at all concentrations and in both high- and low-processivity traces.
source: Furthermore, long stalls (sometimes exceeding tens of seconds in duration) around 10–15 bp are evident at all concentrations and in both high- and low-processivity traces.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Stalling behavior around 10-15 bp has been reported previously and attributed to XPD's encounter with GC-rich regions at this position in the hairpin.
source: This stalling behavior has been reported previously (Qi et al., 2013) and attributed to XPD's encounter with GC-rich regions—which are more difficult to unwind due to higher base-pairing energy—at this position in the hairpin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All low-processivity bursts exhibit stalls around 10-15 bp, after which XPD either backslides to the base of the hairpin or dissociates.
source: All low-processivity bursts exhibit these stalls, after which XPD either backslides to the base of the hairpin or dissociates, ending the burst.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: XPD can continue unwinding past 25 bp after a long stall and be categorized as 'high processivity'.
source: However, we have observed XPD to continue unwinding past 25 bp after a long stall and be categorized as 'high processivity'.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Unwinding behavior within each burst category remains the same over all RPA2 concentrations.
source: Unwinding behavior within each burst category remains the same over all RPA2 concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The averaged unwinding traces exhibit the same behavior independent of RPA2 concentration.
source: The averaged unwinding traces exhibit the same behavior independent of RPA2 concentration.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Low-processivity bursts all display stalls at ~10 bp, whereas high-processivity bursts unwind past this region.
source: Low-processivity bursts all display stalls at ~10 bp, whereas high-processivity bursts unwind past this region.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The velocity of high-processivity bursts is consistently higher than for low-processivity bursts at the ~10 bp position.
source: While XPD on average slows down near 10 bp due to the high GC content of this section of the hairpin, the velocity of high-processivity bursts is consistently higher than for low-processivity bursts at this position.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in velocity are insignificant across varying [RPA2] within the same processivity category.
source: On the other hand, differences in velocity are insignificant across varying [RPA2] within the same processivity category.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both low- and high-processivity burst durations remain constant with RPA2 concentration.
source: We also find that both low- and high-processivity burst durations remain constant with RPA2 concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, light-colored and open data points, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: High-processivity unwinding in the absence of RPA2 is indistinguishable from that in the presence of RPA2.
source: Our results show that high-processivity unwinding in the absence of RPA2 is indistinguishable from that in the presence of RPA2 and likewise for low-processivity unwinding.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: All parameters quantified by burst in the same processivity category are independent of [RPA2].
source: All parameters we quantified by burst in the same processivity category are independent of [RPA2].
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: [RPA2] increases the probability of high-processivity bursts.
source: Instead, [RPA2] increases the probability of high-processivity bursts.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: High- and low-processivity unwinding correspond to intrinsic states of XPD, with RPA2 increasing the likelihood of XPD being in a state competent for high-processivity unwinding.
source: These findings suggest that high- and low-processivity unwinding correspond to intrinsic states of XPD, with RPA2 increasing the likelihood of XPD being in a state competent for high-processivity unwinding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that processivity types are independent of RPA2 concentration.

claim: Point mutations in the homologous Thermoplasma acidophilum XPD were identified that yielded increased unwinding activity and force generation.
source: In a previous study, point mutations in the homologous Thermoplasma acidophilum XPD were identified that yielded increased unwinding activity and force generation (Pugh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mutant FacXPDH202A targets the site analogous to H198 in TacXPD that had been shown to elicit the largest positive effect on unwinding activity.
source: We thus synthesized the mutant FacXPDH202A, which targeted the site analogous to H198 in TacXPD that had been shown to elicit the largest positive effect on unwinding activity (Pugh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The residue H202 is located on domain HD1, within a secondary binding site thought to interact with the translocating strand of DNA in the groove between HD1 and the FeS domains.
source: This residue is located on domain HD1, within a secondary binding site thought to interact with the translocating strand of DNA in the groove between HD1 and the FeS domains (see Figure 1a, black DNA contacts behind the FeS domain).
evidence: This is supported by structural information and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: XPDH202A exhibits higher processivity than wt XPD and can regularly unwind the entire hairpin during its multiple bursts on the DNA hairpin.
source: Like wild-type (wt) XPD, XPDH202A also unwinds DNA in repeated bursts. However, on its own, XPDH202A exhibits higher processivity and can regularly unwind the entire hairpin during its multiple bursts on the DNA hairpin.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The average burst processivity of XPDH202A greatly exceeds that of wt XPD and is also slightly higher than that of wt XPD in the presence of 10 nM RPA2.
source: As shown in the scatter plot in Figure 5b, the average burst processivity of XPDH202A greatly exceeds that of wt XPD and is also slightly higher than that of wt XPD in the presence of 10 nM RPA2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The fraction of high-processivity bursts for XPDH202A is much higher than for wt XPD and comparable to that for wt XPD with RPA2.
source: Similarly, the fraction of high-processivity bursts for XPDH202A is much higher than for wt XPD and comparable to that for wt XPD with RPA2 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The unwinding processivity of XPDH202A does not increase appreciably in the presence of 10 nM RPA2.
source: Interestingly and unlike wt XPD, the unwinding processivity of XPDH202A does not increase appreciably in the presence of 10 nM RPA2 (Figure 5b, c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b and 5c.

claim: The processivity of XPDH202A (alone or in the presence of RPA2) is similar to that of wt XPD with RPA2, suggesting that RPA2 elicits the same effect on XPD as the H202A mutation.
source: Overall, the processivity of XPDH202A (alone or in the presence of RPA2) is similar to that of wt XPD with RPA2, suggesting that RPA2 elicits the same effect on XPD as the H202A mutation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of processivity between XPDH202A and wt XPD with RPA2.

claim: RPA2 did not reduce the frequency of XPD backsteps and backslides.
source: However, identifying XPD backsteps and backslides in unwinding traces (e.g., Figure 3—figure supplement 2) shows that RPA2 did not reduce their frequency.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a marginal increase in the fraction of backsteps from 19 ± 1% to 25 ± 1% as RPA2 increased from 0 to 50 nM.
source: There is a marginal increase in the fraction of backsteps (which we defined as steps between −2 and 0 bp) from 19 ± 1% to 25 ± 1% and almost no change in the fraction of backslides (defined as steps smaller than −2 bp) from 18 ± 1% to 19 ± 1% as RPA2 increased from 0 to 50 nM.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis.

claim: There is almost no change in the fraction of backslides from 18 ± 1% to 19 ± 1% as RPA2 increased from 0 to 50 nM.
source: There is a marginal increase in the fraction of backsteps (which we defined as steps between −2 and 0 bp) from 19 ± 1% to 25 ± 1% and almost no change in the fraction of backslides (defined as steps smaller than −2 bp) from 18 ± 1% to 19 ± 1% as RPA2 increased from 0 to 50 nM.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis.

claim: The mean duration of either the low- or high-processivity bursts does not increase with RPA2, as predicted by a sequestration mechanism.
source: However, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b, we do not observe the mean duration of either the low- or high-processivity bursts to increase with RPA2, as predicted by a sequestration mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Direct RPA–helicase interactions have been detected for the superfamily 2 human helicases WRN, BLM, RECQ, FANCJ, and SMARCAL1 and shown to increase helicase activity.
source: Direct RPA–helicase interactions have been detected for the superfamily 2 human helicases WRN, BLM, RECQ, FANCJ, and SMARCAL1 and shown to increase helicase activity (Cui et al., 2004; Gupta et al., 2007; Bétous et al., 2013; Brosh et al., 1999; Brosh et al., 2000; Doherty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The inability of the non-cognate T4 gp32 to enhance XPD unwinding strongly suggests that specific interactions between XPD and RPA2 are essential.
source: The inability of the non-cognate T4 gp32 to enhance XPD unwinding (Pugh et al., 2008 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4) strongly suggests that specific interactions between XPD and RPA2 are essential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that gp32 does not enhance XPD unwinding.

claim: Formation of an XPD–RPA2 complex may require pre-assembly on DNA.
source: While no strong interactions between FacXPD and FacRPA2 have been reported in solution (Pugh et al., 2008), formation of an XPD–RPA2 complex may require pre-assembly on DNA.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the lack of observed interactions in solution.

claim: The residue H202 lies within a secondary DNA binding site on the HD1 domain, in the groove between the HD1 and FeS domains.
source: As shown in Figure 6a, XPD has several secondary DNA binding sites, and the residue H202 lies within one site on the HD1 domain, in the groove between the HD1 and FeS domains (Kuper et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: XPD–ssDNA contacts at the secondary site are believed to be important for DNA fork positioning and to play an inhibitory role, acting as a throttle to unwinding.
source: XPD–ssDNA contacts at this site are believed to be important for DNA fork positioning and to play an inhibitory role, acting as a throttle to unwinding (Pugh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Disruption of contact points by mutagenesis in both TacXPD and FacXPD enhances unwinding.
source: Disruption of contact points by mutagenesis in both TacXPD (Pugh et al., 2012) and FacXPD (Figure 5) enhances unwinding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Structural analysis of XPD and homologs maps ~5 nt of the translocating DNA strand to the secondary site between the DNA fork at the FeS domain and the entry pore into the motor core.
source: Structural analysis of XPD and homologs maps ~5 nt of the translocating DNA strand to this secondary site between the DNA fork at the FeS domain and the entry pore into the motor core (Qi et al., 2013; Kokic et al., 2019; Pugh et al., 2012; Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: RPA2 binding of 5 nt of ssDNA at the secondary site could interfere with the inhibitory XPD–ssDNA contacts and activate XPD unwinding to a similar extent as mutation.
source: We propose that RPA2 binding of these 5 nt of ssDNA could interfere with the inhibitory XPD–ssDNA contacts at this secondary site and activate XPD unwinding to a similar extent as mutation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data and structural information.

claim: XPDH202A processivity is comparable to that of wt XPD in the presence of RPA2, and RPA2 does not enhance XPDH202A processivity further.
source: Such a mechanism is consistent with our observation that XPDH202A processivity is comparable to that of wt XPD in the presence of RPA2, and that RPA2 does not enhance XPDH202A processivity further (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prior single-molecule measurements showed that individual XPD exhibits 5 bp backward/forward step pairs, attributed to the transient release/recapture of 5 nt of ssDNA from the secondary site.
source: In further support of this model, prior single-molecule measurements (Qi et al., 2013) showed that individual XPD exhibits 5 bp backward/forward step pairs (see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2; dark blue box), attributed to the transient release/recapture of 5 nt of ssDNA from the secondary site.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of RPA2, the frequency of 5 bp backward/forward step pairs decreases.
source: In the presence of RPA2, we observe the frequency of such events to decrease (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; compare dark blue box for 0 nM to 50 nm RPA2), consistent with the idea that RPA2 may affect DNA contacts to this regulatory site.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fact that gp32 has no effect on XPD despite having a similar footprint as RPA2 indicates that binding of ssDNA at the secondary site is insufficient by itself; specific protein–protein contacts between RPA2 and XPD must also be required.
source: Lastly, the fact that gp32 has no effect on XPD despite having a similar footprint as RPA2 indicates that binding of ssDNA at the secondary site is insufficient by itself; specific protein–protein contacts between RPA2 and XPD must also be required.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that gp32 does not enhance XPD unwinding.

claim: XPD can adopt two intrinsic states, one competent for high-processivity unwinding and the other not.
source: XPD can adopt two intrinsic states, one competent for high-processivity unwinding and the other not.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: The two states of XPD correspond to different conformations of the DNA fork in its interactions with the secondary binding site on XPD.
source: We propose that these two states correspond to different conformations of the DNA fork in its interactions with the secondary binding site on XPD.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data and structural information.

claim: Both states are populated independently of RPA2; highly processive unwinding activity can occur in the absence of RPA2 and is indistinguishable from that detected in the presence of RPA2.
source: Both states are populated independently of RPA2; highly processive unwinding activity can occur in the absence of RPA2 and is indistinguishable from that detected in the presence of RPA2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: RPA2 does not assist XPD unwinding by directly destabilizing the duplex, but rather by transiently shifting the equilibrium toward the state competent for high processivity.
source: RPA2 does not assist XPD unwinding by directly destabilizing the duplex, but rather by transiently shifting the equilibrium toward the state competent for high processivity.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: RPA2 binding to ssDNA at the fork interferes with its interactions with the secondary site in a similar way as the H202A mutation, activating high-processivity unwinding.
source: RPA2 binding to ssDNA at the fork interferes with its interactions with the secondary site in a similar way as the H202A mutation, activating high-processivity unwinding.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: k1 increases linearly with RPA2 concentration.
source: Finally, we find that k1 increases linearly with RPA2 concentration (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The linear dependence of k1 on [RPA2] suggests that a simple second-order reaction between RPA2 and the XPD–DNA complex shifts the equilibrium to the high-processivity state.
source: The linear dependence on [RPA2] suggests that a simple second-order reaction between RPA2 and the XPD–DNA complex shifts the equilibrium to the high-processivity state and rules out mechanisms in which multiple RPA2 bind cooperatively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear dependence of k1 on [RPA2].

claim: The linear dependence of k1 on [RPA2] rules out mechanisms in which multiple RPA2 bind cooperatively.
source: The linear dependence on [RPA2] suggests that a simple second-order reaction between RPA2 and the XPD–DNA complex shifts the equilibrium to the high-processivity state and rules out mechanisms in which multiple RPA2 bind cooperatively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear dependence of k1 on [RPA2].

claim: The second-order rate constant obtained from the slope of k1 vs. [RPA2] is (1.5 ± 0.5)×10^7 M^−1 s^−1.
source: The second-order rate constant obtained from the slope of k1 vs. [RPA2], (1.5 ± 0.5)×107 M−1 s−1, is approximately eight times smaller than our estimated rate constant for RPA2 binding to bare ssDNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), expected since DNA-bound XPD should partially block RPA2 access to ssDNA.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the data.

claim: The second-order rate constant for RPA2 binding to the XPD–DNA complex is approximately eight times smaller than the estimated rate constant for RPA2 binding to bare ssDNA, expected since DNA-bound XPD should partially block RPA2 access to ssDNA.
source: The second-order rate constant obtained from the slope of k1 vs. [RPA2], (1.5 ± 0.5)×107 M−1 s−1, is approximately eight times smaller than our estimated rate constant for RPA2 binding to bare ssDNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), expected since DNA-bound XPD should partially block RPA2 access to ssDNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of rate constants.

claim: The intercept of 1–2 × 10^−2 s^−1 provides a basal rate of interconversion between the two processivity states in the absence of RPA2.
source: The intercept of 1–2 × 10−2 s−1 provides a basal rate of interconversion between the two processivity states in the absence of RPA2.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the data.

claim: The fraction of high-processivity XPD bursts measured vs. RPA2 is well fit by the kinetic model with no additional fitting parameters.
source: This simple kinetic model can also be compared to our other results. The fraction of high-processivity XPD bursts measured vs. RPA2 (Figure 4c) is well fit by the model with no additional fitting parameters (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the fit shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The average burst duration is well described by the kinetic model.
source: Likewise, the average burst duration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) is well described by the same model (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the fit shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Recent studies of SF2 helicase RecQ suggest a similar inhibitory role of a secondary DNA binding site, which could plausibly be modulated by DNA binding proteins.
source: The general mechanism described here for XPD may apply broadly to other helicases. Recent studies of SF2 helicase RecQ (Harami et al., 2017) suggest a similar inhibitory role of a secondary DNA binding site, which could plausibly be modulated by DNA binding proteins.
evidence: This is a speculation based on citation to prior literature.

claim: Studies on SF1 helicases UvrD, Rep, and PcrA have shown that alternate conformations of one subdomain strongly affect activity, particularly processivity.
source: Likewise, studies on SF1 helicases UvrD, Rep, and PcrA have shown that alternate conformations of one subdomain strongly affect activity, particularly processivity (Comstock et al., 2015; Arslan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Interactions with protein partners favoring particular conformations may provide a mechanism for activating processive unwinding.
source: Interactions with protein partners favoring particular conformations may provide a mechanism for activating processive unwinding (Arslan et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior literature.
